title: How models see clothing
notes: We want to predict a clothing category from a picture. A catalogue could use that prediction to help organise new items. This is supervised multiclass classification: our target is one of ten clothing labels. Logistic regression is our baseline. We compare it with a nearest-neighbour classifier and a CNN to see what the extra complexity buys us and which mistakes remain. Think of someone searching the catalogue for a shirt. A mistake on that item matters to the search even if the catalogue is mostly correct. Keep that example in mind when we get to the overall result.

title: Fashion-MNIST
notes: Fashion-MNIST gives us 70,000 labelled grayscale images in a common format. Its balance makes accuracy easy to interpret: each category has equal representation and we give each mistake equal cost. Accuracy is our primary metric. We also report macro-F1 and class recall because a good overall score can hide a weak category. Look at the shirt and pullover examples. Even with labels and a clean background, you have very little detail to work with. Balance gives us equal numbers of examples to compare across categories.

title: From an image to 784 numbers
notes: Each image has 784 unsigned eight-bit pixel values. The target is an integer category label. Our exploration found no missing values, invalid labels or exact duplicates in the development data. About half the training pixels are zero. We kept the observations and divided intensities by 255. That fixed transformation needs no fitted statistics. Logistic regression and kNN receive flattened pixels; the CNN receives the original grid in one channel. Across training images the mean intensity was about 73 out of 255. Black is a valid measurement, so treating zeros as missing would alter the garment images. We applied the division and reshape directly in code. A fitted scikit-learn Pipeline would matter if, for example, we estimated a mean to subtract. That mean would have to come from training alone.

title: Keeping the comparison fair
notes: The publisher supplied the 10,000-image test set. We split the remaining 60,000 into 48,000 training and 12,000 validation images. We took the first split from StratifiedGroupKFold. Stratification preserved class proportions, and grouping would have kept identical images together. Each category was exactly ten percent of every split, so resampling was unnecessary. We used one validation holdout for tuning. We fitted the models on training data, compared candidate settings on validation, and froze the checkpoints before scoring the test set once. Follow Shirt across the three rows. The count changes from 4,800 to 1,200 to 1,000, yet the share stays at ten percent. Five-fold cross-validation would move the validation role through all five folds and average the results. We never made that rotation. Keeping the selected checkpoints also means the tested models are exactly the ones whose validation behaviour we inspected.

title: Logistic regression: weighted pixels
notes: Logistic regression gives each pixel a weight for each class. Adding the weighted pixels and intercept gives a class score. The heatmap shows contributions to the predicted score. Of four L2 regularisation settings, C equal to 0.1 had the highest validation accuracy. Our baseline reached 87.42 percent on training and 84.33 percent on test. Its three-point gap is modest. A linear score also limits how this model can combine neighbouring pixels into patterns. Look at the coloured map beside the coat. A pixel contributes its intensity multiplied by the weight for this particular class. Changing which class we explain would change the weights, even though the photograph would stay the same. This gives us a baseline whose calculation we can trace.

title: kNN: the nearest examples
notes: For kNN we tried three, five and nine neighbours. Three won on validation. Here two of the three nearest images are pullovers, so the coat is misclassified. To measure training accuracy, each image voted using only the three nearest other images. That gave 85.27 percent, close to 85.04 percent on test. Its test advantage over the logistic baseline was just 0.71 percentage points. Watch the three neighbours appear before looking at the vote. The model only sees distances between pixel vectors. Dividing every coordinate by 255 scales every distance equally, so the same three images would still be nearest. And three only beat five by seven validation images.

title: Inside the CNN
notes: The CNN keeps the grid. The first convolution learns 32 local filters and the second learns 64. Pooling reduces the spatial dimensions, then a 128-unit dense layer combines the features. We used dropout of 0.25 and restored epoch 12. At that checkpoint accuracy was 95.67 percent on training and 91.79 percent on test. That is a 7.46-point gain over our baseline. The remaining train-to-test gap motivated a closer look at the learning curves. Follow one channel from the first block. The same filter is applied at different positions, so its response can appear in different parts of the image. Now switch channels. The input stays fixed while the response changes. We can see where each filter responds. Naming one a sleeve detector would take more evidence. We trained on raw scores using cross-entropy and applied softmax to display the ranking.

title: Which pixels matter?
notes: For this coat, gradient saliency highlights pixels where a small change would most affect the Coat score. Occlusion asks what happens to the same score when we cover a patch. As the patch moves, the readout shows the change in the raw score. Both maps describe sensitivity for this image. Later we will use SHAP to measure signed contributions to a probability. Watch the original score stay fixed as the covered score changes. The difference belongs to that patch, that fill colour and that target class. A bright patch alone cannot tell us what makes a real garment a coat.

title: Choosing the settings
notes: We chose settings on validation accuracy. Within each CNN run we restored the epoch with lowest validation loss. Across configurations, the wider CNN without weight decay won. The two wider versions were very close across three seeds, and weight decay had higher mean shirt recall. We retained the original accuracy-first choice. Those seeds measure training variation on the same split. This is where the catalogue example matters. If finding shirts were our first priority, the weight-decay run would deserve another look. Changing the rule after seeing the test results would give us a different experiment.

title: When training stops helping
notes: Training loss continued falling after epoch 12. Validation loss reached its minimum there, so later epochs improved training fit without improving that criterion. Training stopped at epoch 17 and restored epoch 12. That divergence is evidence of overfitting with further training. Move along the curve from twelve to seventeen. The optimiser is still improving its fit to training images. The validation loss gives us a reason to stop trusting that improvement on new inputs.

title: Final test performance
notes: The summary shows the size of the improvement. kNN gains less than one point over logistic regression. The CNN gains more than seven and also leads on macro-F1. It had already won on validation; final testing confirmed the choice. Which items does it still miss? Out of the same ten thousand images, the baseline got 8,433 right and the CNN got 9,179 right. The difference is 746 additional correct predictions in total. It tells us nothing yet about which categories gained.

title: Accuracy varies by category
notes: Each confusion-matrix row starts with a thousand actual items. Read across a row to see the predictions. The CNN recognises 99 percent of bags but only 67.6 percent of shirts. Equal class sizes make that difference particularly easy to interpret. Try reading the shirt row before looking at the percentage. Only the diagonal counts as a correctly identified shirt. The other cells show where actual shirts went. Reading down the shirt column would answer a different question about predicted shirts.

title: Shirt recall and directional errors
notes: Of the thousand actual shirts, 324 were missed. Look at the first pair: 127 shirts were called T-shirt or top, while only 63 T-shirts or tops were called shirt. The same asymmetry appears for coats and pullovers. Similar outlines are a plausible explanation at this low resolution. The counts establish the direction of the errors; the images alone cannot establish their cause. Suppose you inspect only items that the catalogue tagged as shirts. You find 676 real shirts among 817 predictions, about 83 percent precision. A customer searching that catalogue still misses 324 actual shirts. That difference between precision and recall is why I would show both numbers to someone deciding whether to use the model.

title: Which regions push the CNN toward Coat?
notes: Both SHAP plots explain the CNN's Coat probability. On the left, each dot is one validation image. Its horizontal position shows how much that quadrant raised or lowered the probability. Colour gives its average brightness. Across these 100 images, upper right has the largest average absolute effect. On the right is one actual shirt predicted as Coat. Starting at the training-reference average of 14.0 percent, all four quadrants push toward Coat, reaching 58.3 percent. For this shirt, lower right contributes most, about 15.5 percentage points. The answer depends on our region boundaries and reference images.

title: What the experiment cannot establish
notes: We used one validation split, so repeated choices could adapt to those images. The CNN also differs from the other models in capacity and training, so the comparison cannot isolate the benefit of convolution alone. Fashion-MNIST contains small, standardised images. My next experiment would evaluate the frozen CNN on independently labelled phone photos with different lighting and backgrounds. A second question would need a different experiment. To test whether convolution itself helps, we could compare against a dense network with similar capacity, on the same split and training budget. That would address architecture. The phone-photo experiment addresses a change in the images people actually submit.

title: The CNN performed best overall
notes: The CNN was the best of our three models on this benchmark. It improved test accuracy by 7.46 points over logistic regression. But if a catalogue particularly needs reliable shirt labels, overall accuracy hides a practical weakness: the CNN misses about a third of actual shirts. That is the result I would investigate before relying on it for new photographs. For a catalogue team, I would ask what a missed shirt costs compared with an incorrect shirt tag. That answer would determine the metric for the next round of model selection. This experiment gives us a measured starting point for that conversation. Thank you. What questions do you have?

title: How did you prevent leakage?
notes: Fit the classifiers. Divide raw pixel intensities by the known maximum of 255; this uses no estimated statistics. Choose C, k, CNN settings and checkpoint. All models use identical source indices. Only the first split from StratifiedGroupKFold was used. Freeze all three checkpoints, verify their hashes and validation predictions, then score once. Exact development/test overlaps: zero.

title: How was kNN training accuracy measured?
notes: For each of the 48,000 fitted images, exclude its own index and search the other 47,999 images. Three Euclidean neighbours, one vote each. A three-way tie goes to the lowest class ID, matching the classifier. 40,931 ÷ 48,000 = 85.27%. Validation: 85.38%. Test: 85.04%. These close scores give little evidence of a large generalisation gap.

title: Why keep the epoch-12 CNN?
notes: Validation loss reached its minimum at epoch 12. Training stopped at epoch 17 and restored that checkpoint. Validation accuracy chose the wider CNN without weight decay. The original seed-42 checkpoint was already selected. Mean accuracy: 92.400% without weight decay and 92.339% with it. Mean shirt recall favoured weight decay: 78.94% vs. 75.81%. All runs used one split.

title: What do these SHAP values measure?
notes: The frozen CNN’s Coat probability. One feature is a 14 × 14 quadrant. Absent quadrants come from the same reference image. Evaluate all 16 subsets of the four quadrants, averaging each over 20 training images (two per class). Average each region’s marginal change over possible orders. The baseline plus four signed contributions recovers each prediction. The beeswarm covers ten validation images per class. Other backgrounds or region boundaries can change the values; mixed images may look artificial.
